Before I write it up, one bigger choice is still open: how the guide itself gets built. The answer decides where the recordings live and what a volunteer sees when they upload one. This is a project-sized piece of work, so it gets a full written design once we settle this.

I see three ways to build it:

1. **Add the guide to your current website, with the recordings stored in the site's own files.** Each code opens an exhibit page on the existing Eleventy site. Volunteers upload through a simple admin page. The clean-up runs each time the site rebuilds. This needs no new services. But 120 audio files, growing each year, make the site heavy to store and rebuild. Each upload also means a wait of several minutes before it goes live.
2. **Add the guide to your current website, with the recordings in separate file storage.** The exhibit pages are the same as in (1). A volunteer's upload goes to cloud storage, and a small program cleans it up as soon as it arrives. The recording then goes live without a site rebuild. The site stays light and volunteers see results quickly. The cost is a second service with a small monthly bill, and someone must look after it.
3. **Use an off-the-shelf audio guide service.** This means the least to build. But it has monthly fees and gives you less control over the look. Welsh support varies by product, and the guide sits apart from your website.

I recommend (2). It keeps the visitor pages on the site you already run. It also gives volunteers a quick upload with no technical steps, and it keeps the audio out of the website's files.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Eleventy builds every page ahead of time. Anything stored in the site's files is part of each build and each deploy.
- Audio is large compared with web pages. Keeping it apart from the site means a new recording doesn't rebuild 60 exhibit pages.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Which way do you want to go?
